new_entities.name: Supervised exercise after chemotherapy for breast cancer
aliases: post-chemotherapy exercise in breast cancer survivors
new_entities.description: Structured exercise participation after breast cancer treatment, especially in survivorship or post-chemotherapy care.

new_entities.name: Recurrence risk
new_entities.description: Risk that previously treated cancer returns locally, regionally, or at distant sites during follow-up.

edges.effect_quant: A meta-analysis of five cohorts found lower recurrence risk at >=7.5 MET-h/week versus 0-3 MET-h/week (HR 0.65, 95% CI 0.58 to 0.73), with newer prospective data showing DRFI benefit above about 5 MET-h/week.
edges.population: women with primary breast cancer in post-diagnosis or survivorship follow-up
edges.mechanism: Post-treatment exercise may reduce recurrence risk through lower insulin signaling, less adiposity-driven inflammation, and improved immune-metabolic control during survivorship. The signal appears dose-responsive up to a moderate activity threshold rather than requiring extreme training loads.
edges.summary: The strongest evidence for recurrence reduction comes from post-diagnosis physical activity cohorts rather than randomized supervised programs, but the direction is fairly consistent. That makes the evidence supportive for supervised post-chemotherapy exercise as a survivorship strategy, while still leaving some uncertainty about how much of the benefit comes from the structured supervision itself versus simply being more active after treatment.
edges.caveats: These data are observational and mostly use recreational physical activity rather than formal exercise-therapy programs. Confounding by baseline health, treatment tolerance, or healthier survivor behavior cannot be fully excluded, so the recurrence signal is encouraging but not strictly causal in the trial sense.

evidence.citation: Miyamoto T et al 2022 Curr Oncol Rep
evidence.notes: Effect of Post-diagnosis Physical Activity on Breast Cancer Recurrence: a Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.

evidence.notes: Exercise after diagnosis of breast cancer in association with survival.
